subtopics.title: Engineering, Environment & Society
subtopics.subtitle: Engineers in national development, environmental impacts, sustainability, EIA and IEE

concepts.text: Engineering and Society

Engineering turns scientific knowledge into roads, bridges, hydropower, water supply, telecommunication networks and software that raise living standards. In a developing country such as Nepal, engineers drive national development: they plan and build infrastructure, deliver public services, create jobs and support industry. Because engineering works last for decades and affect many people who never signed the contract, engineers carry a responsibility to society and the environment that goes beyond satisfying the client.
Roles of engineers in society and national development:
items: Planning, designing, building and maintaining infrastructure (transport, energy, water, communication, housing).
Using local resources and technology appropriate to local conditions, skills and budgets.
Advising government and communities on technical choices, safety, costs and risks.
Protecting public health and safety through sound design, supervision and compliance with codes.
Innovation and entrepreneurship that create employment and reduce dependence on imports.
Disaster preparedness, reconstruction and climate adaptation of infrastructure.

concepts.text: Environmental Impacts of Engineering

rows: Dust, vehicle and generator exhaust, brick kilns
Water spraying, cleaner kilns, emission control
Settling basins, treatment plants, minimum environmental flow
Slope cutting, landslides, quarrying, spoil dumping
Bioengineering, designated spoil sites, slope protection
Forest clearing, habitat fragmentation, fish barriers
Route change, compensatory plantation, fish ladders

concepts.text: Sustainable Development

The Brundtland Commission (1987) defined sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. For engineers this means balancing three pillars, often called the triple bottom line: economic viability, social equity and environmental protection. Life-cycle thinking (from raw material through construction, operation and disposal) and the 3Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle) are practical tools for sustainable design.
Mitigation hierarchy applied to environmental impacts (in order of preference):
items: Avoid: choose a location, route or design that does not cause the impact at all.
Minimise: reduce the duration, intensity or extent of impacts that cannot be avoided.
Restore or rehabilitate: repair affected areas after construction (replanting, reinstating land).
Offset or compensate: counterbalance residual impacts elsewhere (compensatory plantation, cash or land compensation).

concepts.text: Environmental Assessment in Nepal

The Environment Protection Act, 2076 (2019) and the Environment Protection Rules, 2077 require proponents to carry out an environmental study before implementing listed projects. Depending on the size, type and sensitivity of the proposal, the study is a Brief Environmental Study (BES), an Initial Environmental Examination (IEE) or a full Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). The applicable schedules and thresholds are set in the Rules and are subject to amendment, so always check the current version.

rows: Projects with limited, largely predictable impacts
Projects with potentially significant or wide impacts
Detailed study of alternatives, impacts and mitigation
EIA report with environmental management plan

concepts.text:
Typical EIA process (concept level)
1. Screening      - decide whether BES, IEE or EIA is required
2. Scoping        - identify key issues; prepare terms of reference
3. Baseline study - physical, biological, socio-economic, cultural data
4. Impact prediction and evaluation (e.g. magnitude x importance)
5. Alternatives and mitigation measures
6. Public consultation / public hearing
7. Report preparation and review, approval by the competent authority
8. Environmental monitoring and auditing during construction and operation
Climate, Disaster and Social Considerations
Nepal-specific considerations engineers must address:
items: Earthquake risk: the 2072 (2015) Gorkha earthquake showed the cost of non-engineered construction.
Floods, landslides and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) threaten roads, bridges and hydropower.
Climate change shifts rainfall and river flows, so designs need adaptation margins.
Social impacts: land acquisition, resettlement, livelihoods, cultural heritage and gender and inclusion.
Public participation builds ownership, surfaces local knowledge and reduces later conflicts and delays.

concepts.plainText: E = A x EF (emission = activity data x emission factor)

concepts.text: The emission-factor method estimates greenhouse gas emissions of an activity. For example, if a construction site burns 2,000 litres of diesel and the emission factor is about 2.68 kg CO2 per litre, emissions are roughly 5,360 kg, or about 5.4 tonnes of CO2. Such estimates help compare design alternatives and report a project's carbon footprint.

formulas.plainText: Impact score = magnitude x importance (Leopold-matrix style)

notes.text: Remember the order screening, scoping, baseline, prediction, mitigation, consultation, review, monitoring. MCQs often ask which step decides whether an IEE or EIA is needed: that is screening.

Under the Environment Protection Act, 2076 the three levels of study are BES, IEE and EIA. The project thresholds that trigger each level are in the schedules of the Environment Protection Rules, 2077 and are subject to amendment.

Do not confuse EIA with an environmental audit. EIA predicts impacts before a project is approved; an audit checks after implementation whether the mitigation measures were actually carried out and worked.

formulas.title: GHG emission estimate
formulas.description: Emissions equal the activity quantity (e.g. litres of fuel, kWh) multiplied by its emission factor.

formulas.title: Impact significance score
formulas.description: In matrix methods such as the Leopold matrix, an impact's significance is rated from its magnitude and its importance.

formulas.title: Total matrix impact
formulas.description: Summing the scores of all activity-environment interactions gives an overall score for comparing alternatives.

flashcards.front: What are the three pillars of sustainable development?
flashcards.back: Economic viability, social equity and environmental protection, often called the triple bottom line.

flashcards.front: What levels of environmental study does Nepal's Environment Protection Act, 2076 provide for?
flashcards.back: Brief Environmental Study (BES), Initial Environmental Examination (IEE) and Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), chosen by project type and scale as set in the Rules.

flashcards.front: What is scoping in an EIA?
flashcards.back: The step that identifies the key environmental and social issues to study and produces the terms of reference for the assessment.

questions.questionText: A proposed large hydropower project is expected to cause significant and wide-ranging environmental and social impacts. Which environmental study is appropriate?
options: No study, only a construction permit
questions.explanation: Projects with potentially significant impacts need a full EIA with detailed impact prediction, alternatives, mitigation and public hearing. An audit is a post-implementation check, not an approval study.

questions.questionText: Which definition of sustainable development was given by the Brundtland Commission (1987)?
options: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Development that maximises GDP growth while treating environmental costs as externalities
Development that halts all use of non-renewable resources immediately
Development financed entirely by domestic resources
questions.explanation: The Brundtland report 'Our Common Future' defined sustainable development in terms of intergenerational equity: meeting present needs without compromising future generations.

questions.questionText: A construction site uses 2,000 litres of diesel. Taking an emission factor of 2.68 kg CO2 per litre, the estimated CO2 emission is:
questions.explanation: E = A x EF = 2,000 x 2.68 = 5,360 kg = 5.36 tonnes of CO2.

questions.questionText: According to the mitigation hierarchy, what should an engineer try first when a road alignment would pass through a sensitive wetland?
options: Avoid the impact by choosing an alternative alignment
Plant trees elsewhere as an offset
questions.explanation: The mitigation hierarchy is avoid, minimise, restore, then offset. Avoidance through alternative siting or design is always preferred first.

questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of a public hearing during an EIA?
options: To fix the contract price with the contractor
To select the project consultant by open bidding
To let affected people and stakeholders express concerns and provide input on impacts and mitigation
To obtain the final design approval from the municipality
questions.explanation: Public hearing is a public-participation tool: it informs stakeholders and collects their views and local knowledge so that impacts and mitigation are properly addressed.

subtopics.title: Professional Ethics & Codes of Conduct
subtopics.subtitle: Ethics, morals and law; duties of engineers; conflicts of interest; codes of conduct

concepts.text: Ethics, Morals and Law

rows: Personal beliefs of right and wrong shaped by upbringing, culture and religion
Systematic principles of right conduct, often for a group or profession
Rules made by the state that everyone must obey

concepts.text: Law sets the minimum acceptable behaviour; ethics usually asks for more. An act can be legal but unethical (for example, exploiting a loophole to use inferior material that just meets a weak specification) or, occasionally, ethical but technically in breach of an outdated rule. Professional ethics is the set of standards that members of a profession accept because society trusts them with specialised knowledge that affects public safety.
Duties of an Engineer
An engineer owes duties to several parties; public safety comes first:
items: To the public: hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public and protect the environment.
To the client or employer: act as a faithful agent, give honest advice, keep information confidential and avoid conflicts of interest.
To the profession: uphold its dignity, work only within competence, give credit to others, and not injure colleagues' reputation falsely.
To oneself: continue learning and maintain professional competence throughout one's career.

concepts.text: Key Ethical Issues

rows: Personal interest could bias professional judgement
Disclose to client or employer; withdraw if needed
Do not disclose without consent unless public safety requires
Working only in areas of qualification
Decline or obtain expert help outside competence
Presenting another's work or design as one's own
Exposing wrongdoing that endangers the public
Use internal channels first, then external authorities

concepts.text: Whistle-blowing is the act of reporting illegal, unsafe or unethical practice by one's own organisation. It is justified when serious harm to the public is likely, the engineer has documented evidence, and internal channels have been tried or would be useless. Responsible whistle-blowing avoids personal grudges, sticks to facts and uses the proper authorities.
Codes of Conduct

A code of conduct or code of ethics is a written set of rules that a professional body expects its members to follow. It gives guidance in difficult situations, protects the public, and provides a basis for disciplinary action. In Nepal, the Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055 (1998) requires registered engineers to follow the code of conduct prescribed by the Council, and a breach can lead to disciplinary action including removal of the name from the register. The Nepal Engineers' Association also has its own code of ethics for members.
Common elements of engineering codes of conduct (NEC code at concept level):
items: Maintain honesty, integrity and impartiality in professional work.
Work only in fields of competence and sign only documents prepared or checked by oneself.
Give priority to public safety, health and the environment.
Avoid corruption, bribery and undue influence; disclose conflicts of interest.
Keep client information confidential and respect intellectual property.
Do not practise engineering without valid registration.

concepts.text: Resolving Ethical Dilemmas

Steps for resolving an ethical dilemma
1. Recognise the ethical issue and get the facts
2. Identify stakeholders and who is affected
3. List the options (including creative middle ways)
4. Test each option: law, code of conduct, public safety,
   fairness, 'would I be comfortable if it were published?'
5. Choose, act and document the decision
6. Review the outcome and learn from it

concepts.plainText: S_j = sum of (w_i x s_ij), weighted score of option j

concepts.text: A weighted decision matrix can support step 4: each option j is scored on criteria such as safety, legality, cost and stakeholder fairness, each score is multiplied by the criterion weight, and the totals are compared. It structures thinking, but a clear breach of law or of public safety rules out an option regardless of its total score.

notes.text: When an MCQ asks for the engineer's first or highest duty, choose the option about the safety, health and welfare of the public. Duties to client and employer come after that.
Confidentiality is not absolute. If keeping a client's secret would put the public in danger, the duty to public safety takes priority.
Disclosure is the standard remedy for a conflict of interest: inform the client or employer in writing, and step aside from the decision if the conflict cannot be managed.

formulas.title: Weighted decision score
formulas.description: Scores each option in an ethical or technical decision by weighting its rating on each criterion.

formulas.title: Risk exposure
formulas.description: Probability times impact, used to judge how serious a safety concern is before deciding to escalate it.

flashcards.front: How do ethics and law differ?
flashcards.back: Law is the minimum standard enforced by the state; ethics sets principles of right conduct that often ask for more than the law.
When serious harm to the public is likely, there is documented evidence, and internal channels have been tried or would clearly fail.

flashcards.front: What can happen to a registered engineer who breaches the NEC code of conduct?
flashcards.back: The Council can take disciplinary action under the NEC Act, 2055, which can include removing the engineer's name from the register.

questions.questionText: According to engineering codes of ethics, an engineer's paramount obligation is to:
options: Protect the reputation of fellow engineers
Hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public
questions.explanation: Codes of ethics place public safety, health and welfare above all other duties, including those to client, employer and colleagues.

questions.questionText: An engineer on a bid evaluation committee finds that one bidder is a company owned by her brother. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Disclose the relationship to the procuring entity and withdraw from evaluating that bid
Continue evaluating but give the brother's company an average score
Say nothing, because she is confident she can be impartial
questions.explanation: This is a conflict of interest. The ethical response is to disclose it and recuse herself so that the evaluation remains impartial.

questions.questionText: A site engineer discovers that the contractor is using under-strength reinforcement in a school building, and his manager tells him to ignore it. What should he generally do first?
options: Post the evidence on social media immediately
Ignore it, since the manager is responsible
Document the evidence and raise the issue formally through higher internal channels, going to the authorities if it is not corrected
questions.explanation: Responsible whistle-blowing starts with documented facts and proper internal escalation, then external authorities if the danger is not addressed. Public safety cannot be ignored.

questions.questionText: Which statement about ethics and law is correct?
options: Law sets a minimum standard, while ethics often requires conduct beyond what the law demands
Ethics applies only to doctors and lawyers, not engineers
Codes of ethics have no link to disciplinary action
questions.explanation: Law is the enforced minimum. Professional ethics often requires more, and professional codes are the basis for disciplinary action by the professional or regulatory body.

questions.questionText: A consulting engineer copies large parts of another firm's design report into his own report and submits it under his name without acknowledgement. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Presenting another's work as one's own without credit is plagiarism, a breach of honesty and of respect for intellectual property in engineering codes.

subtopics.title: Regulatory Environment & Contemporary Issues in Engineering
subtopics.subtitle: Laws, codes and standards for engineering in Nepal, and today's professional challenges

concepts.text: Why Engineering Is Regulated

Engineering works can kill people when they fail, so the state regulates who may practise, how structures are designed, how public money is spent, how workers are protected and how the environment is safeguarded. The regulatory environment is the combined set of Acts, regulations, codes, standards and institutions within which an engineer works. Knowing it is part of professional competence.

rows: Registration of engineers, recognition of education, conduct
Building Act, 2055 and National Building Code (NBC)
Safe design and construction of buildings
BES, IEE, EIA and pollution control
Employment conditions and occupational safety and health
Registration and governance of companies, including consulting firms
Quality, safety and fair dealing in goods and services

concepts.text: National Building Code and Standards

The National Building Code of Nepal is a set of NBC documents covering materials, loads, seismic design, masonry, reinforced concrete, and guidelines for small buildings. NBC 105 deals with seismic design of buildings; its current version, NBC 105:2020, was revised after the 2015 Gorkha earthquake. Municipalities enforce the code through building permits under the Building Act, 2055, and the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction (DUDBC) is responsible for the code at the federal level.

concepts.plainText: V = Cd x W (base shear = design seismic coefficient x seismic weight)

concepts.text: In the equivalent static method of seismic codes, the design horizontal base shear V is the seismic weight W of the building multiplied by a design coefficient Cd. The coefficient depends on the seismic zone, soil type, the structure's natural period, its importance and its ductility, and is taken from the current code. For example, Cd = 0.08 and W = 5,000 kN give V = 400 kN.
Standards and quality infrastructure:
items: Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology (NBSM) is the national standards body: it formulates Nepal Standards (NS), runs certification, operates testing laboratories and maintains measurement standards.
The NS certification mark under the Nepal Standards (Certification Mark) Act, 2037 shows that a product conforms to the relevant Nepal Standard.
Engineers also use international standards (ISO, IEC, IS, BS, ASTM, IEEE) where no Nepal Standard exists or when a contract specifies them.

concepts.text: Contemporary Issues in Engineering

rows: Skilled engineers migrate abroad; local capacity weakens
Poor materials, weak supervision, early failures
Enforcement of codes, testing, qualified supervision
Cost overruns, substandard work, lost public trust
Floods, landslides, GLOF risk to infrastructure
Upskilling, digital project tools, open data
Attacks on banks, utilities, government systems
Secure design, incident response, legal framework

concepts.text: Cyber law is relevant to computer engineers: the Electronic Transactions Act, 2063 (2008) gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures and defines computer-related offences. Other contemporary concerns include delayed projects, low maintenance budgets, unplanned urbanisation, the gap between academia and industry, and the need for continuing professional development.
Engineer's Responsibility within the Regulatory Framework
Practical duties arising from the regulatory environment:
items: Hold valid NEC registration before practising engineering.
Design to current codes and standards and record the edition used.
Follow procurement rules strictly when handling public contracts.
Ensure required environmental studies and safety measures are in place before work starts.
Keep up to date, because Acts, regulations and codes are amended.

formulas.plainText: Compliance rate = compliant items / inspected items x 100%

notes.text: Match each law to its purpose: NEC Act 2055 for registration, Public Procurement Act 2063 for public purchasing, Environment Protection Act 2076 for EIA/IEE, Labour Act 2074 for workplace safety, Electronic Transactions Act 2063 for cyber offences.
Seismic coefficients, zone factors and other code values change with revisions of NBC 105. Always use the current edition rather than memorised numbers.
Section numbers, fees and thresholds in Nepali Acts and regulations change through amendments. Learn the purpose and structure of each law, not specific figures.

formulas.title: Seismic base shear
formulas.description: Equivalent static design base shear equals the code's design coefficient times the building's seismic weight.

formulas.title: Code compliance rate
formulas.description: Share of inspected buildings or items that meet the code, used to monitor enforcement.

flashcards.front: What does NBC 105 cover in the National Building Code of Nepal?
flashcards.back: Seismic design of buildings; the current version NBC 105:2020 was revised after the 2015 earthquake.

flashcards.front: What are the main functions of NBSM?
flashcards.back: It prepares Nepal Standards, certifies products with the NS mark, operates testing laboratories and maintains national measurement standards.

flashcards.front: What is brain drain and why does it matter for Nepal's engineering sector?
flashcards.back: Brain drain is skilled professionals emigrating; it reduces local expertise and weakens design, supervision and innovation at home.

questions.questionText: Which body is Nepal's national standards body responsible for formulating Nepal Standards and granting the NS certification mark?
options: Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology
questions.explanation: NBSM prepares Nepal Standards, runs product certification (NS mark), testing and metrology. NEC regulates engineers, and NEA is a professional society.

questions.questionText: In the National Building Code of Nepal, NBC 105 deals with:
questions.explanation: NBC 105 is the seismic design code for buildings in Nepal, revised as NBC 105:2020 after the Gorkha earthquake.

questions.questionText: Using the equivalent static method, a building has a seismic weight of 5,000 kN and a design seismic coefficient Cd of 0.08. The design base shear is:
Which law primarily governs the procurement of works, goods and consulting services by public entities in Nepal?
questions.explanation: The Public Procurement Act, 2063 and Public Procurement Regulations, 2064 set the procedures for public procurement to ensure competition, transparency and accountability.

questions.questionText: A hacker breaks into a municipality's revenue system and alters records. Which Nepali law most directly defines such computer-related offences?
questions.explanation: The Electronic Transactions Act, 2063 recognises electronic records and digital signatures and defines computer-related offences such as unauthorised access and alteration of data.

subtopics.title: Occupational Health & Safety
subtopics.subtitle: Hazards, risk assessment, hierarchy of controls, PPE, accident rates and OHS law

concepts.text: What Occupational Health and Safety Means

Occupational health and safety (OHS) is the discipline of preventing work-related injuries and illnesses and promoting workers' physical, mental and social well-being. A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm; risk is the combination of the likelihood that harm occurs and the severity of that harm. Construction sites, factories, power installations and even computer offices all contain hazards that engineers must identify and control.

rows: Noise, heat, falls, moving machinery, electricity, radiation
Cement dust, solvents, fumes, battery acid
Poor posture, repetitive keyboard work, heavy lifting
Stress, long hours, harassment, job insecurity

concepts.text: Risk Assessment and Hierarchy of Controls

Five steps of risk assessment
1. Identify the hazards
2. Decide who might be harmed and how
3. Evaluate the risk (likelihood x severity) and decide on controls
4. Record the findings and implement the controls
5. Review and update the assessment regularly or after changes
Hierarchy of controls, from most to least effective:
items: Elimination: remove the hazard completely (e.g. prefabricate at ground level so no work at height is needed).
Substitution: replace with something less hazardous (e.g. water-based paint instead of solvent-based).
Engineering controls: isolate people from the hazard (guards, ventilation, earth-leakage circuit breakers, guardrails).
Administrative controls: change the way people work (procedures, training, permits to work, job rotation, signs).
Personal protective equipment (PPE): the last line of defence, used when other controls cannot reduce risk enough.

rows: Being struck by vehicles, falls from height

concepts.text: Accident Causation, Reporting and Rates

Accidents result from unsafe acts (not using PPE, bypassing guards) and unsafe conditions (unguarded machines, poor lighting, faulty wiring), often with management system failures behind them. Heinrich's accident pyramid suggests that for about every major injury there are many minor injuries and hundreds of near misses, so reporting and investigating near misses prevents serious accidents. Every accident should be reported, investigated for root causes, recorded and followed by corrective action.

concepts.plainText: FR = lost-time injuries x 1,000,000 / man-hours worked
SR = man-days lost x 1,000,000 / man-hours worked

concepts.text:
Worked example (IS 3786 style rates)
Workers 500, 8 h/day, 300 days -> 500 x 8 x 300 = 1,200,000 man-hours
Lost-time injuries = 6, man-days lost = 180
FR  = 6 x 10^6 / 1,200,000        = 5
SR  = 180 x 10^6 / 1,200,000      = 150
Incidence rate = 6 x 1000 / 500    = 12 per 1000 workers
FSI = sqrt(FR x SR / 1000) = sqrt(0.75) = 0.87
Safety Organisation and OHS Law in Nepal

The Labour Act, 2074 (2017) contains a chapter on occupational safety and health. At concept level it requires employers to provide a safe and healthy workplace, arrange protective equipment and training, prevent hazards from machines and chemicals, and form a safety and health committee with worker representation in enterprises above a prescribed size. Workers must follow safety instructions and use the protective equipment provided. Specific thresholds and details are in the Act and Labour Rules, 2075 and are subject to amendment.
Electrical and computer-workplace safety:
items: Use proper earthing, correctly rated fuses or circuit breakers and residual current devices (RCD/ELCB).
Isolate and lock out supply before maintenance; test that circuits are dead before touching them.
Never overload sockets; keep cables tidy to avoid tripping and insulation damage.
For display-screen work: adjustable chair, monitor top at about eye level, wrists neutral, regular breaks to prevent eye strain and repetitive strain injury.
Server rooms need fire detection, suitable (clean-agent or CO2) extinguishers and controlled access.

notes.text: Order of the hierarchy of controls: elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE. MCQs often ask for the most effective control (elimination) or point out that PPE is the last resort.
Rate conventions differ: IS 3786 uses 1,000,000 man-hours as the base, while OSHA incidence rates use 200,000 hours. Read the base given in the question before calculating.
Under the IS 3786 and ANSI conventions a fatality or permanent total disability is charged as 6,000 man-days lost when computing the severity rate.

formulas.title: Frequency rate
formulas.description: Number of lost-time injuries per million man-hours worked.

formulas.title: Severity rate
formulas.description: Man-days lost due to injuries per million man-hours worked.

formulas.title: Incidence rate
formulas.description: Injuries per thousand workers in the period.

formulas.title: Frequency severity index
formulas.description: Combines frequency and severity into one index for comparing safety performance.

flashcards.front: List the hierarchy of controls from most to least effective.
flashcards.back: Elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, personal protective equipment.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hazard and a risk?
flashcards.back: A hazard is anything that can cause harm; risk combines the likelihood of the harm happening with its severity.

flashcards.front: Why are near misses reported and investigated?
flashcards.back: Near misses share causes with serious accidents (Heinrich's pyramid), so fixing them prevents future injuries.

questions.questionText: In the hierarchy of hazard controls, which measure is the most effective?
questions.explanation: Elimination removes the hazard completely and sits at the top of the hierarchy; PPE and signs rely on human behaviour and are least effective.

questions.questionText: A site employs 250 workers for 48 hours a week over 50 weeks and records 9 lost-time injuries. The accident frequency rate per million man-hours is:
A factory worked 800,000 man-hours in a year and lost 240 man-days due to injuries. The severity rate per million man-hours is:
questions.explanation: SR = 240 x 10^6 / 800,000 = 300 man-days lost per million man-hours.

questions.questionText: A data-entry operator develops wrist pain from long hours of repetitive typing at a badly positioned keyboard. This hazard is classified as:
questions.explanation: Repetitive movements and poor workstation posture are ergonomic hazards, leading to repetitive strain injuries.

questions.questionText: Installing a machine guard and local exhaust ventilation to isolate workers from a hazard is an example of which level of control?
questions.explanation: Engineering controls physically separate people from the hazard (guards, ventilation, interlocks) without relying on worker behaviour.

subtopics.title: Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA): Roles & Responsibilities
subtopics.subtitle: NEA as Nepal's professional engineering society, its roles, and how it differs from NEC

concepts.text: What NEA Is

The Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA) is the professional society of engineers in Nepal, established in 2019 BS (1962 AD). It is a non-governmental, non-profit and non-political organisation that brings together engineers of all disciplines. Unlike the Nepal Engineering Council, NEA is not a statutory regulator: it does not license engineers, but it represents them, develops the profession and promotes ethical practice.
Broad objectives of NEA (concept level):
items: Promote the engineering profession and the professional interests and welfare of engineers.
Advance engineering knowledge, research and technology relevant to Nepal.
Encourage high standards of professional conduct and ethics among members.
Contribute engineering expertise to national development and to public policy.
Build cooperation with national and international professional organisations.

concepts.text: Membership

Membership of NEA is voluntary. Engineers holding recognised engineering qualifications can join, and the constitution provides different membership categories (for example general and life membership, and honorary membership for distinguished persons). Members are organised into discipline-based divisions or societies and regional branches or centres, which run activities closer to members. The exact categories and conditions are set in NEA's constitution and may change.
Roles and Responsibilities

rows: Represents engineers' views to government on policy and law
Code of ethics for members; promotes integrity
Works with NEC, universities and international bodies
Volunteers expertise, e.g. in disaster response

concepts.text: NEA versus NEC

rows: Registered association with its own constitution
Registration, recognition of education, conduct and discipline
Can take disciplinary action and remove names from the register

concepts.text: The two bodies complement each other. NEC protects the public by controlling who may practise and by recognising engineering programmes; NEA strengthens the profession from within by developing and representing its members. An engineer in Nepal typically registers with NEC because the law requires it, and joins NEA to grow professionally.
Measuring a Professional Society's Reach

Annual reports of associations often describe growth in membership or events with a compound annual growth rate. For an illustrative case, if members grow from 10,000 to 14,641 in 4 years, g = (1.4641)^(1/4) - 1 = 0.10, i.e. 10% per year. The figures here are an example only, not NEA's actual membership.
Responsibilities of an engineer as an NEA member:
items: Follow NEA's code of ethics as well as the NEC code of conduct.
Take part in professional development and share knowledge with juniors and students.
Uphold the dignity of the profession and avoid bringing it into disrepute.
Contribute to society through voluntary technical service where possible.

notes.text: If an MCQ asks which body registers engineers, recognises engineering degrees or can cancel a registration, the answer is NEC, not NEA. NEA is the professional society established in 2019 BS (1962 AD).
Do not memorise unverified figures about NEA such as current membership numbers, fee amounts or committee sizes; they change and are set by NEA's own constitution and decisions.
NEA membership is voluntary, while registration with NEC is a legal requirement for practising engineering in Nepal under the NEC Act, 2055.

formulas.title: Compound annual growth rate
formulas.description: Average yearly growth rate of a quantity such as membership over t years.

formulas.title: Participation rate
formulas.description: Share of members taking part in an event or programme, a simple indicator of engagement.

flashcards.front: When was the Nepal Engineers' Association established?
flashcards.back: In 2019 BS (1962 AD), as the professional society of engineers in Nepal.

flashcards.front: What is the key difference between NEA and NEC?
flashcards.back: NEA is a voluntary, non-governmental professional society; NEC is the statutory regulator under the NEC Act, 2055 that registers engineers and takes disciplinary action.
Professional development through training and conferences, publications and knowledge sharing, and advocacy for engineers and the profession, alongside promoting ethics.

questions.questionText: The Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA) was established in:
questions.explanation: NEA was founded in 2019 BS (1962 AD). 2055 BS is the year of the Nepal Engineering Council Act, which created the statutory regulator.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly describes the Nepal Engineers' Association?
options: It is a non-governmental professional society of engineers
It is the statutory body that issues licences to practise engineering
It is a government department under the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure
It is an international standards organisation
questions.explanation: NEA is a non-governmental, non-profit professional society. Licensing and registration are functions of the Nepal Engineering Council.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a function of NEA?
options: Advocating engineers' interests to the government
Removing an engineer's name from the statutory register for misconduct
questions.explanation: Disciplinary removal from the register is a power of the Nepal Engineering Council under the NEC Act, 2055. NEA's roles are professional development, publications and advocacy.

questions.questionText: An engineer says: 'I have joined NEA, so I no longer need to register with NEC to practise.' This statement is:
options: Correct, because NEA membership replaces NEC registration
Incorrect, because NEA membership is voluntary while NEC registration is legally required to practise
Correct only for engineers working in the private sector
Incorrect, because NEA membership is compulsory and NEC registration is optional
questions.explanation: NEA is a voluntary professional society; practising engineering in Nepal requires registration with NEC, the statutory regulator.

questions.questionText: A young engineer wants to update her knowledge through seminars, present a technical paper and network with senior professionals. Which organisation is primarily meant for such activities?
options: Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology
Department of Labour and Occupational Safety
questions.explanation: Professional development, conferences, publications and networking are core roles of NEA as the professional society of engineers.
